title: Agentic Report Generator
tagline: An experiment in letting a local AI research a database and write its own reports
summary: At my 2026 internship I tried building an AI that could take a question, dig through a big database on its own, make charts and maps, and write up a report. It worked, but the small models we could run locally weren't smart enough to do it reliably, so it stayed an experiment.

sections.heading: The idea
body: Instead of picking tables, writing SQL, exporting results and building a report by hand, you'd just ask a question in plain English. Simple questions got a short answer, and asking for a report started a longer process.

sections.heading: How it worked
body: I split it into steps, because one AI call couldn't do everything at once. First it planned the report and the questions to answer. Then it researched: it looked up the tables it needed, ran read-only queries, and saved each result as a finding. Last, it wrote each section from those saved findings, so the report was based on real numbers instead of whatever the model remembered.
codeBlocks:
QUESTION
   ↓
UNDERSTAND  →  research plan + report outline
   ↓
RESEARCH    →  schema search → read-only SQL → saved findings
   ↓                              ↘ charts + maps
COMPOSE     →  one grounded section at a time
   ↓
REPORT

sections.heading: Charts and maps
body: The AI could ask for charts and maps, but it never wrote plotting code. It just described what it wanted and the server drew it. Maps could show heat maps, points or clusters of signals.

sections.heading: Keeping it safe
body: The AI could write its own queries, but only ones that read data, with a row limit and a timeout, on a read-only database connection. So even a bad query couldn't change anything.

sections.heading: Why it stayed an experiment
body: Small models were fast but stopped researching too early or wrote shallow reports. Bigger ones did better but were way too slow on the computer I had. I added retries, better prompts and tests, but that can't make a model smarter than it is. It was still worth doing, because it taught me how to tell when the problem is my code and when it's the model.
